section_summary: This section closes one copy of the July 1945 report “Trade Unions and Collective Bargaining in Japan” with rosters, statistical appendices, and extracts from laws used to repress labor organization. A September 4, 1945 memorandum then transmits another copy of the report, whose cover, contents, recommendations, historical survey, and discussion of Japanese industrial relations occupy the remainder of the section. The report advocates free democratic unions and collective bargaining under the occupation while recommending controls on stoppages in industries essential to military operations and security.

subfiles.title: Trade Unions and Collective Bargaining in Japan: Appendices A–D
subfiles.about: The concluding appendices document prewar unions, membership and dispute statistics, and laws that obstructed or repressed organized labor.
subfiles.summary: The surviving portion begins with the end of a roster of principal unions and their leaders, affiliations, membership, and organizational units. Statistical tables trace union membership from 1926 to 1939, its distribution by industry and prefecture, and the incidence, causes, and adjustment of labor disputes through 1940. The final appendix reproduces provisions of the Peace Preservation Law, thought-surveillance regulations, the National Mobilization Law, the Public Peace Police Law, and the Police Crimes Punishment Law that the report recommends abrogating or amending under military government.

subfiles.title: Trade Unions and Collective Bargaining in Japan
subfiles.doc_type: confidential report and Civil Affairs Guide
subfiles.about: The report analyzes Japanese labor organization and industrial relations and proposes an occupation policy toward unions, bargaining, strikes, and dispute settlement.
subfiles.summary: After its cover and contents, the report recommends protecting democratic unions, permitting collective bargaining, repealing repressive laws, freeing labor prisoners, dissolving Sampo, and creating a military-government labor section. It surveys the history and structure of left-wing, conservative, company, and fascist unions and describes employer associations, patriotic societies, the Harmonization Society, Sampo, and the wartime militarization of labor. It then examines paternalism, police repression, strikes, collective bargaining, shop committees, and arbitration mechanisms, including underground wartime labor unrest. The final pages in this section anticipate severe postwar hardship and renewed union activity and begin setting out general occupation principles for stable, democratic labor relations while protecting essential operations.
